content.title: About
content.content: Chocolate candy with a candy shell (5118) are small sweets consisting of a soft chocolate filling coated with a thin, crisp sugar shell. They offer a sweet, slightly caramel‑like flavor and a pleasant texture that combines smooth chocolate with a crunchy outer layer.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The sugar shell is created by drizzling hot sugar syrup over the candy, which then quickly hardens.
These candies first appeared in Europe in the 19th century as a way to extend the shelf life of chocolate treats.
Colored shells are achieved by adding food‑grade dyes to the sugar syrup.
Chocolate candies with shells are often used as decorations for desserts and cakes.
In some countries they are called “candy‑coated chocolates” because of their bright outer coating.

items.title: Source of antioxidants
items.content: Chocolate, especially dark chocolate, contains flavonoids that help combat free radicals.

items.title: Contains trace minerals
items.content: The product provides small amounts of magnesium and iron, essential for normal body functions.

items.title: Quick energy boost
items.content: The simple sugars give an immediate source of energy, useful during intense physical activity.

items.title: Allergy to chocolate or milk proteins
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to cocoa or dairy components.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Excessive consumption can contribute to weight gain and increase the risk of dental caries.

items.title: Possible trans‑fat content
items.content: Some manufacturers use partially hydrogenated oils, which may be harmful to heart health.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The candies can be enjoyed as a standalone snack, added to ice cream, yogurt, or used to garnish desserts. They are conveniently packaged for on‑the‑go consumption.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in a cool, dry place in an airtight container to prevent the sugar shell from becoming sticky. At temperatures above 25 °C the shell may soften.

egg-substitute-omelet-scrambled-or-fried.title: Egg substitute, omelet, scrambled or fried, no added fat

content.title: About
content.content: Egg substitute is a ready‑to‑use blend that lets you make omelets, scrambled eggs or fried dishes without using real eggs and without added fat. It typically contains plant proteins, starch, flavorings and sometimes B‑vitamins to mimic the taste and texture of eggs.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Egg substitute is a staple in vegan cooking as an alternative to chicken eggs.
The blend can be based on soy, pea or hemp protein.
Some brands add turmeric or natural colorants to give a yellow hue similar to yolk.
It is shelf‑stable in dry form; preparation only requires adding water.
Using the substitute helps reduce cholesterol and saturated fat intake.

items.title: Rich in plant protein
items.content: The mix provides a complete amino‑acid profile, supporting muscle maintenance.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Cooking without added oil keeps the dish low in calories.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: Added B12, B2 and folate help replicate the nutritional value of eggs.

items.title: Heart‑friendly
items.content: Absence of cholesterol and saturated fats makes it safe for cardiovascular health.

items.title: Allergy‑friendly for egg‑allergic individuals
items.content: People with egg allergy can safely use the product.

items.title: Soy or pea protein allergy
items.content: Some substitutes are soy‑ or pea‑based and may trigger reactions in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Missing micronutrients
items.content: Unlike real eggs, the product may contain lower amounts of vitamin D and choline.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Certain brands add salt for flavor; check the label if you need to limit sodium.

items.title: Texture variations
items.content: Improper water‑to‑mix ratios can result in a dry or overly runny final product.

content.title: How to Cook
content.content: Combine the substitute with water according to package directions (usually 1 tsp mix + 120 ml water). Pour the batter onto a pre‑heated non‑stick pan without oil and cook like a regular omelet or scrambled eggs until set.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the dry powder in an airtight container in a cool, dry place away from moisture and direct sunlight. Once opened, use within about 6 months.

content.title: About
content.content: A waffle is a light baked product made from batter cooked in a waffle iron. The reduced‑fat version contains roughly half the fat of regular waffles while retaining the characteristic crisp exterior and soft interior. It works well for breakfast, a snack, or a dessert.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Waffles originated in Europe in the 16th century and quickly became popular because they are easy to make.
There are more than 30 types of waffle batters, including Belgian, American and Asian variations.
Waffles are often used as a base for "waffle cake" and "waffle sandwich" dishes.
Fat reduction is achieved by replacing part of the butter with plant oils and adding aerating agents.
Waffles store well: their low moisture content helps them stay crunchy for a long time.

items.title: Reduced fat content
items.content: Lower fat makes the product more suitable for calorie‑controlled diets.

items.title: Source of carbohydrates
items.content: Waffles provide quick‑digesting carbs that rapidly replenish energy after exercise.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: The batter is usually fortified with thiamine, riboflavin and niacin, supporting metabolism.

items.title: Lower sugar level
items.content: Reduced‑fat versions often contain less added sugar as well.

items.title: Versatile pairing
items.content: Can be topped with fruit, yogurt, or nut butter for a more balanced meal.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: The batter contains wheat flour, so it is not suitable for people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: Rapidly absorbable carbs may cause a blood‑sugar spike in individuals with diabetes.

items.title: Additive content
items.content: Fat‑reduction often involves food additives that can trigger individual reactions.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Warm the waffle briefly in a toaster or microwave. Serve with berries, low‑fat cottage cheese, honey, nut butter, or low‑fat yogurt. It also pairs well with savory toppings such as ham and cheese.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep waffles in an airtight container in a cool, dry place. For longer storage, refrigerate or freeze them to maintain crispness. Before use, check that they are free of moisture and mold.
